o: We must crawl a web graph starting from `startUrl`, visiting only pages whose hostname equals the hostname of `startUrl`, never visiting a URL twice, and using multiple threads because `getUrls` is a blocking network call (~15ms each). Example 1: starting at `http://news.yahoo.com/news/topics/` we parse it, get yahoo and google links, filter out google, and keep expanding until all 4 yahoo URLs are collected. Example 2: the start page only links to other hostnames, so the answer is just `startUrl` itself. Constraints (≤1000 nodes) mean correctness and deduplication matter more than raw throughput, but single-threaded DFS/BFS times out, so concurrency is mandatory. The key synchronization needs are: a thread-safe visited set, a way to know when no more work exists (all workers idle), and filtering by hostname.
k: Hostname extraction: strip "http://" and take everything before the next '/' — this defines which links to crawl.
Deduplication must happen atomically: use a concurrent set or a lock so two threads never crawl the same URL.
Termination detection: track active tasks; when the queue is empty AND no worker is processing, crawling is done.

a.n: Approach 1: Concurrent BFS with a Blocking Queue
a.i: Spawn N worker threads that share a blocking queue of URLs to crawl and a synchronized visited set. Each worker takes a URL, fetches its links, filters by hostname, and adds unseen ones. A counter of in-flight tasks lets us detect completion: when the queue is empty and zero tasks are being processed, all reachable pages have been crawled.
s: Extract the target hostname from startUrl; seed queue with startUrl and mark it visited.
Each worker loops: poll the queue with a timeout; if empty and activeTasks == 0, exit.
For each polled URL, increment activeTasks, call parser.getUrls, filter same-hostname unvisited URLs, add them under a lock, decrement activeTasks.
Join workers and return the visited list.
a.t: O(V + E) work across all threads — each URL parsed once, each edge examined once; wall-clock time divided roughly by the number of workers since getUrls blocks on I/O.
a.sp: O(V + E) for the visited set, queue, and per-page link lists.

a.n: Approach 2: Executor Service / Task-based Crawl (Java-idiomatic optimal)
a.i: Instead of long-lived polling workers, submit one task per discovered URL to a fixed thread pool. Each task parses its page and submits children. Completion is detected when the count of unfinished tasks drops to zero (e.g., via Phaser or an AtomicInteger + executor shutdown), which removes busy-waiting and scales cleanly.
s: Create a fixed thread pool and a Phaser/counter registered once for the initial task.
Submit a task for startUrl; each task registers itself before spawning children.
Task body: filter same-hostname unvisited URLs (atomic set add), register and submit child tasks.
When a task finishes, arrive/deregister; when the phase count hits zero, shut down the pool.
Await termination and return the visited set as a list.
a.t: O(V + E) total work; tasks are dispatched dynamically so there is no idle polling overhead.
a.sp: O(V + E) for the visited set plus O(depth × V) worst-case stack/futures.

w: **Which approach to pick:** In an interview, lead with the concurrent BFS/producer-consumer design (Approach 1) since it maps directly onto classic patterns (blocking queue, completion detection), then mention the task-submission variant (Approach 2) as the cleaner production-style refinement. **Pitfalls:** forgetting to deduplicate *atomically* (two threads can both pass a `contains` check); comparing full URL prefixes instead of extracting the exact hostname (`http://news.yahoo.com` vs `http://news.yahoo.com.evil.com` trap); deadlocking or spinning forever because termination requires *both* an empty queue and zero in-flight tasks; calling `getUrls` while holding the lock (serializes I/O and defeats multithreading). **Edge cases:** startUrl with no path, self-loops/cycles in the graph, and all links pointing off-hostname. **Follow-ups:** at 10k nodes / 1B URLs, partition by hostname hash across machines (consistent hashing), use a distributed queue (Kafka/SQS) and a shared dedup store (Redis/bloom filters); handle node failure with heartbeats and task reassignment/leases; the crawl is done when the global queue is empty and all machines report zero in-flight tasks (distributed barrier/countdown).
